strengths: The paper proposes a mathematically grounded distillation objective for ResShift, with Proposition 3.1 providing a tractable reformulation that avoids backpropagating through the full teacher-training loop, and with clear connections to VSD and inverse bridge matching.

Empirical evaluation is extensive: RealSR, RealSet65, ImageNet-Test, DIV2K-Val, and DRealSR, with fidelity, full-reference perceptual, and no-reference metrics. RSD improves substantially over SinSR on perceptual metrics and is competitive with or better than larger T2I-based methods such as OSEDiff and SUPIR on several benchmarks.

The efficiency advantage is significant and well documented: one-step inference, 174M parameters, 0.059s inference time, and 539MB GPU memory, versus much larger T2I-based models. This makes the contribution practically relevant for efficient real-world SR.

Reproducibility is strong for a methods paper: appendices include dataset links/licenses, hyperparameters, training time, pseudocode, baseline checkpoints, and implementation details. The paper also discusses limitations, failure cases, and potential societal impact.

Ablations on multistep training and supervised losses support the design choices and clarify the perceptual-distortion trade-off. The distill-only variant helps isolate the effect of the proposed distillation loss.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate at best. The proposed loss is closely related to existing distillation objectives such as VSD, SiD, FGM, and IBMD; the authors themselves show reformulations that resemble SiD/FGM and a discrete IBMD loss. The main novelty is adapting this class of objectives to ResShift with SR-specific supervised losses, which may be viewed as an incremental task-specific contribution.

The central theoretical assumption in Eq. (6), that matching optimal ResShift denoisers is equivalent to matching data distributions, is plausible but not rigorously established under finite data, latent VAE compression, and imperfect optimization. The paper does not provide formal identifiability conditions or bounds on the approximation error.

Important one-step diffusion SR baselines are missing. TSD-SR, a cited target-score distillation method for real-world SR, is not compared experimentally, and AddSR is only evaluated in an appendix. A stronger comparison to recent one-step SR distillation methods would better support the claims.

Evaluation fairness is imperfect. The main comparison with OSEDiff uses 256x256 training crops for RSD while OSEDiff is trained/evaluated at 512x512; the authors acknowledge this but still draw broad 'on par with SOTA' conclusions. Perceptual gains rely heavily on no-reference metrics (CLIPIQA, MUSIQ), which can favor generative artifacts, and RSD is not always best on these metrics.

The paper sometimes overstates improvements. RSD 'outperforms the teacher by a large margin' only on perceptual metrics; it often has lower PSNR/SSIM than ResShift and SinSR. The claims should be qualified as perceptual-distortion trade-off improvements rather than general superiority.

Stability and sensitivity of the training scheme are not fully analyzed. Simultaneously training a generator and a fake ResShift with a GAN loss involves hyperparameters such as K, lambda_1, and lambda_2; no variance/error bars or sensitivity study is provided, leaving questions about robustness and reproducibility across runs.

strengths: Delivers a genuinely practical 1-step SR model: 174M parameters, ~539 MB peak GPU memory, and 0.059 s inference, matching SinSR and roughly 10× cheaper in parameters/memory than T2I-based SR methods such as OSEDiff, while remaining competitive perceptually.

Evaluation is broad and systematic: real (RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR) and synthetic (ImageNet-Test, DIV2K) benchmarks, full-reference and no-reference metrics, plus ablations on multistep training (Table 5) and supervised losses (Table 6), and a self-implemented ResShift-VSD baseline for a controlled comparison.

The derivations are largely correct and the paper is transparent about the algebra: it shows the proposed loss can be rewritten in forms resembling SiD/FGM/IBMD and explicitly derives the tractable variant (Proposition 3.1, Appendix I), enabling an honest conceptual comparison with VSD/ADD.

Reproducibility is fairly good: implementation builds on the public SinSR codebase, hyperparameters, optimizer settings, update schedule (K=5), loss weights, training time, and dataset/model licenses are provided (Appendix C, Tables 7–9).
Limitations, failure cases, and societal-impact discussion are handled honestly (Appendix H), including cases where the method fails relative to T2I priors.
weaknesses: The claimed theoretical novelty is overstated, and the paper itself undermines it: Appendix A.2 states the objective closely resembles SiD and FGM, and A.3 concludes the loss is a discrete variant of the IBMD loss. The 'novel objective' therefore reduces largely to re-instantiating known fake-model/distribution-matching losses in the ResShift/Real-ISR setting, which is a modest contribution.

A substantial part of the improvement over SinSR appears to come from bolting on standard supervised losses (LPIPS from OSEDiff, GAN from DMD2, plus DMD2's K=5 update scheme) rather than from the distillation objective. Table 6 shows adding supervised losses drives the perceptual gains, so the incremental value of L_theta over existing distillation losses is not clearly isolated.

Key comparative claims are selective and do not hold uniformly. On DRealSR (Table 3) RSD is worse than OSEDiff on PSNR (27.40 vs 27.92), SSIM, LPIPS, MUSIQ, and MANIQA, contradicting the broad claim of 'better fidelity' than OSEDiff; the 'on par with SOTA' framing rests on favorable datasets and metrics.

The headline claim of outperforming the teacher 'by a large margin' is misleading: it reflects a perception–distortion trade-off shift, not dominance. PSNR/SSIM relative to ResShift drop on most benchmarks (e.g., Table 1: PSNR 25.91 vs 26.49), so the improvement is confined to no-reference perceptual metrics.

Assumption (6) — that matching the fake and teacher ResShift models implies matching the underlying data distributions — is asserted, not justified, and no analysis is given for why the objective does not sit near zero trivially. Since both the generator and the fake model are initialized from the teacher, the loss is near zero at initialization; the paper provides no evidence or theory explaining what non-trivial learning signal drives the process.

The comparison against AddSR (Appendix F, Table 16) is not clearly apples-to-apples, since AddSR is trained on different data/resolution and a different setup; using it to support '×10 fewer parameters with better results' is therefore weak support.

Statistical reliability of the reported differences is unclear: no variance, seeds, or significance testing are given, and many gaps between RSD and competitors (e.g., CLIPIQA/MUSIQ differences) are small enough to be within run-to-run noise.

There is an internal tension in the loss analysis: the paper argues the joint-distribution loss L_theta is superior to VSD's marginal loss, yet its own derivation (Appendix A.1) shows the gradient of L_theta contains the VSD gradient up to scaling plus stop-gradient-like auxiliary terms, so the practical mechanism of the benefit is not adequately explained.

strengths: Introduces a new distillation objective for ResShift-based SR, with Proposition 3.1 giving a tractable fake-model reformulation and a clear theoretical link to joint-distribution matching rather than marginal matching (VSD).

Achieves 1-step SR with better perceptual metrics than SinSR and competitive perceptual quality versus much larger T2I-based models such as OSEDiff/SUPIR, while using only 174M parameters and about 0.06s inference time.

Provides extensive experiments on real and synthetic benchmarks (RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR, ImageNet-Test, DIV2K) with multiple metrics, complexity analysis, and ablations on multistep training and supervised losses.
The distillation-only variant already improves over SinSR on several perceptual metrics, supporting the value of the proposed core loss beyond the added LPIPS/GAN terms.
Good scholarly practice: appendices include proofs, pseudocode, dataset licenses, detailed experimental settings, limitations/failure cases, societal impact discussion, and an LLM-usage statement.
weaknesses: Theoretical novelty is incremental: the core loss is closely related to existing fake-model distillation methods (VSD, SiD, FGM, IBMD) as acknowledged in the appendix, and the main contribution is an adaptation/extension to ResShift for SR rather than a fundamentally new distillation paradigm.

Comparison with OSEDiff is not fully controlled: RSD is often trained on 256x256 ImageNet while OSEDiff uses 512x512 LSDIR; although the authors note this bias and include some 512x512 results, the main claims of competitive perceptual quality still rely partly on cross-setup comparisons. Recent one-step SR methods such as TSD-SR are not compared in the main tables.

Claims that RSD 'outperforms the teacher by a large margin' are based mainly on no-reference perceptual metrics while PSNR/SSIM drop; no human evaluation is provided, and no-reference metrics can be misleading.

Reproducibility could be stronger: no code release or repository link is provided in the manuscript, and some implementation details (e.g., GAN discriminator architecture, exact metric computation scripts) are only partially specified.

Ablation of key hyperparameters is limited: the sensitivity to the fake-model update count K, the loss weights lambda1/lambda2, and discriminator design is not thoroughly analyzed; no variance/seed analysis is reported for the quantitative results.
